beads.title: Absorb all quad-100 traffic locally in TUN mode instead of handing non-DNS packets to the overlay
beads.description: Upstream's netstack used to intercept traffic addressed to the Tailscale service IP (100.100.100.100 / fd7a:115c:a1e0::53) only for an allow-list of ports -- TCP 53/80/8080 and UDP 53 -- and returned filter.Accept for everything else, letting the packet fall through to the ACL filter and on to wireguard-go, where no peer owns the quad-100 AllowedIP. Upstream removed the allow-list: handleLocalPackets now absorbs every quad-100 packet into netstack regardless of IP protocol or port, 'so such traffic never reaches the conntrack / peer-routing layers', and a companion hittingServiceIP case in acceptTCP cleanly RSTs an unserved quad-100 TCP port instead of falling through to the isTailscaleIP branch that rewrote the dial target to 127.0.0.1:<port>. This repository has the same allow-list, and in TUN transport mode it has the leak upstream closed. ts_runtime::tun_actor's classify_magic_dns returns a query only when the packet is IPv4 AND UDP AND destined to 100.100.100.100:53; anything else takes the Intercept::NotIntercepted arm in up_pump and is sent to the overlay unchanged. tun_actor steers 100.100.100.100/32 into the TUN whenever MagicDNS is enabled, so the host genuinely emits such packets -- a stub resolver speculatively trying DoT on 100.100.100.100:853 is upstream's own cited example. ts_overlay_router then matches the destination against its outbound table, and that table carries a selected exit node's 0.0.0.0/0 as RouteAction::Wireguard(peer) (built in ts_runtime::route_updater), which matches 100.100.100.100. So with an exit node configured -- the configuration this fork exists for -- the node's own service-IP traffic is encrypted and sent to a peer; with no exit node and no CGNAT-covering subnet route it is merely dropped as unrouted, which is why this has gone unnoticed. The decision to make: where to put the absorb. The natural place is classify_magic_dns / plan_intercept, widening it from 'is this a MagicDNS query' to 'is this addressed to the service IP at all', with a new Intercept arm that consumes-and-drops a quad-100 packet that is not a DNS query, so the packet never reaches up.send(). Decide whether an unserved quad-100 TCP port should be silently dropped or answered with a RST, and note that upstream's second half is structurally not applicable here: this tree has no isTailscaleIP-to-host-loopback dial rewrite for such a connection to fall through to. The netstack transport already behaves correctly and should be left alone -- ts_runtime::netstack_actor gives the netstack interface 100.100.100.100 as a local address, so quad-100 terminates there whatever the port or protocol -- but a test asserting that both transports agree is worth having. Test the negative case explicitly: with an exit node's 0.0.0.0/0 in the overlay table, a quad-100 packet that is not UDP/53 must not appear in what the pump forwards. Anti-leak, host-facing. See PORTING.md section B, 'New at this revision'.

beads.title: Set the DNS TC flag on a forwarded reply that exceeds the client's EDNS buffer size
beads.description: Upstream added checkResponseSizeAndSetTC to net/dns/resolver and calls it on every path that returns a UDP answer (the plain UDP forward, the DoH forward, and the TCP-fallback path). If the reply is larger than the EDNS buffer size the request advertised -- or larger than 512 bytes when the request carried no EDNS OPT record, per RFC 1035 -- it sets the TC (truncated) bit in the response header, leaving the body intact, so the stub resolver knows to retry over TCP. This repository already gets this right for the answers it builds itself: ts_dns_wire caps an authoritative response at MAX_UDP_MSG_LEN (512) and sets TC when it has to drop an answer, asserted by oversized_answer_set_sets_tc_and_caps_512. The gap is the forwarded path. ts_runtime::magic_dns's cap_response sets TC only when the upstream reply exceeds MAX_UPSTREAM_RESPONSE (4096) and is chopped mid-message; a reply that sits between the client's own limit and 4096 -- 900 bytes answering a plain non-EDNS query, say -- is relayed verbatim with TC clear, where a Go node would set it. The decision to make: parse the forwarded request's OPT record (the additional section) for its advertised UDP payload size, default to 512 when there is none, and set TC when the reply exceeds that; keep the existing 4096 cap, but do not describe it as a read bound -- it is not one, and it does not bound memory. forward_query reads with recv_from_bytes, which issues Recv { max_len: None }, so the netstack has already copied the whole datagram out before cap_response runs; what bounds the read is the netstack UDP socket's receive ring (netcore::Config::udp_buffer_size, 4 KiB by default and not overridden by ts_runtime), and smoltcp drops a datagram larger than that ring at enqueue rather than delivering it. With the ring and the cap both at 4096, cap_response's truncate-and-set-TC branch cannot fire on any datagram this socket can deliver, so it is defensive today and the new EDNS check would be the only thing that ever sets TC on the forwarded path. Leave the 4096 cap as the relay bound it is -- the two checks compose rather than replace each other -- and if a memory bound is wanted on this path it has to come from the read (a bounded recv, or udp_buffer_size), not from cap_response. ts_runtime::magic_dns already has a question-section walker (the byte range helper used to match a reply to its query) that the OPT lookup can build on, so this needs no new dependency. Decide also whether to apply the check to authoritative replies as well, where ts_dns_wire's unconditional 512 is stricter than a client advertising a larger EDNS size would allow -- stricter is safe, but the two paths currently disagree about where the limit comes from. Test both directions: a plain query whose forwarded reply is over 512 must come back with TC set, and a query advertising a large EDNS size whose reply fits under it must come back with TC clear. Narrow in practice, because the query is forwarded verbatim and a well-behaved upstream honours the EDNS size itself -- but 'the upstream is well-behaved' is exactly the assumption upstream stopped making. Host-facing, not wire-facing. See PORTING.md section B, 'New at this revision'.
